steps.title: In the ground
steps.text: Nearly all niobium comes from one mineral, pyrochlore, in rare volcanic rocks called carbonatites. One deposit, at Araxá in Brazil, supplies most of the world. Deep weathering there has left ore rich enough to dig without blasting.

shares.caption: World reserves, of the quantified total

steps.india: 142,200 t of niobium oxide has been established with rare earths in Gujarat and Rajasthan; blocks in Rajasthan have been auctioned.

steps.title: Mine
steps.text: The Brazilian ore is soft and is dug from open pits. Canada's one mine, in Quebec, is underground.

steps.title: Concentrate
steps.text: The ore is ground and the iron removed with magnets. Fine clay is washed away and the pyrochlore floated. Leaching then strips out phosphorus, lead and sulphur, which steelmakers do not want.

steps.title: Reduce
steps.text: The concentrate is mixed with aluminium powder and iron and ignited. The aluminium takes the oxygen, and the reaction's own heat melts the product into ferroniobium. About nine-tenths of all niobium is sold in this form, made beside the mine.
steps.alt: A small share is purified to oxide and metal, for superalloys and for the niobium-titanium wire in superconducting magnets.
steps.india: The Nuclear Fuel Complex makes reactor-grade and superconductor-grade niobium in small quantities. No ferroniobium is made.

steps.title: Use
steps.text: A few hundred grams of niobium in a tonne of steel make it markedly stronger and tougher, so pipelines, car bodies and bridges can use less steel. Steel takes about 77% of niobium in the United States and jet-engine superalloys 23%. Superconducting niobium wire is the heart of MRI scanners.
steps.india: Steel and superalloy makers; all niobium is imported.

steps.title: Recycle
steps.text: Niobium is not recovered on its own. It returns inside steel scrap, where it is diluted, and inside superalloy scrap, which is remelted.
